I recently installed a set of v-brakes on one of my bikes that was initially set up with cantilevers. First off, let me say that the difference is huge. I know there are people out there who will say that cantilevers are just as good if not better than v-brakes when set up correctly. They will talk about things like modulation and fine tuning the geometry of cantilevers, something you can't do with v-brakes. At first I was mislead by these points, but now I know better.

Cantilever brakes are a pain. They take a lot of time to set up properly. You need to do your homework on them. You really need to know what you're doing. That's a huge drawback. Having spent the time learning about them and fine tuning them, I can honestly say that v-brakes are better in that sense because they mostly just work and are far easier to set up and maintain.

The point about cantilevers having better modulation is true, however I can say from experience that linear pull v-brakes still provide more raw stopping power than a pair of painstakingly adjusted cantilevers. They are more responsive at the lever. Proponents of cantilevers will tell you this is bad. They will actually argue that people who prefer v-brakes because they are more responsive are just noobs, as if having too much braking power is bad, and that modulation is more important, so that it's better to have to squeeze down harder for longer and still get less performance out of your brake anyway. I'm actually angry that people would say such things, because I was mislead by them.

V-brakes just work better, easier, faster.

Since my bike came set up with cantilevers, it has brake levers that are incompatible with v-brakes. A cantilever brake requires a shorter cable pull. V-brakes require levers that are designed to pull about twice the amount of cable. This means that you either have to install new levers when switching from canti to V, or you can use an adapter. The adapter is a double pulley called a Travel Agent, and it's made by Problem Solvers.

The adapter takes the place of the noodle on one of your v-brake arms. It is a real pain to get the cable routed through it correctly. Afterwards, you'll probably need to increase the spring tension on your brake arms to get them to return properly. IIRC, this was noted in the instructions. I had to set the spring tension of the brake arms close to maximum. A set of brake bosses will usually have 3 holes next to them for inserting the spring. The top hole is maximum, the bottom is minimum, and the middle is in between. Normally, you'd want to use the middle hole, but with the adapter, I had to use the top one.

Setting up the adapter was totally worth it. Even with the stock pads that came with the v-brakes, and even with the added resistance and slightly sub-optimal pull due to using an adapter instead of a proper v-brake lever, the v-brakes easily perform better than the cantilevers with salmon pads ever did. I'm sold.

At some point, I may get new brake levers to complete the conversion. I don't know how well the adapter will do over time, but for now I think I will be fine.

If you are considering cantilevers over v-brakes, I highly recommend just going with v-brakes. If that's not an option, at least get yourself a set of koolstop salmon pads for your cantilevers. They will help.
V-brakes with an incompatible brake lever and a cable pulley adapter

Nobody really seems to have been interested in this subject, but I wanted to add that I had an idea to reduce the amount of spring tension in the brake arms and it worked beautifully.

When I first installed the travel agent pulley, I had to use the top position for the springs at the brake bosses, which made the brake arm spring tension very high and therefore created more resistance when pulling the brake lever. What I did to fix this was to set the springs back down in the middle slot, unhook them from the brake arms, and then screw the adjusting screws all the way in for maximum tension, which I had been unable to do previously while the springs were fully seated. I then hooked the springs back onto the brake arms and gradually unscrewed the adjusting screws to reduce the spring tension until I found the sweet spot of the lowest possible spring tension while still allowing the brake arms to fully retract.

Now the action on my brake lever is much easier. So there's a little tip for anyone installing one of these pulleys.

Another tip is to unscrew your barrel adjuster several turns before threading the cable through the pulley. After fully installing the cable, playing with the barrel adjuster will allow you to fine-tune the position of the slot on the travel agent. The position of that slot is important.
